newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition to seek tax talks with opposition.
newsitem.headline: German coalition to seek tax talks with opposition.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition will offer to meet the opposition Social Democrats this month for negotiations on a planned tax reform, the party's general secretary Peter Hintze said.

Responding to a comment from SPD faction chief Rudolf Scharping, who said earlier on Thursday he hoped to hold talks in a bid to break a standstill in the tax debate, Hintze told German television "I expect the coalition to offer to talk to the Social Democrats about the tax reform this month."
Hintze said the aim would be to agree a tax relief programme which could start in 1998.
"This is an important project for growth and employment and more jobs," he said.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel signalled compromise on this point on Wednesday, presenting for the first time concrete prosposals that could bring forward the planned income tax reform by one year to 1998.

The government coalition, made up of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the Christian Social Union (CSU) and the Free Democrats (FDP), has proposed a 30 billion mark net tax cut in 1999 that would cut the top rate to 39 percent.

The SPD, which can block parts of the tax reform with its majority in the upper house of parliament, has urged Bonn to bring forward the tax cuts to 1998. It opposes government plans to partly finance the reform by raising value added taxes.
